title: Storage Engines: B-Trees vs LSM
subtitle: Watch the same write travel through a B-tree and an LSM tree, and see where each one pays its cost.
learn: How a B-tree updates a page in place, and why a tiny change rewrites a whole page
How an LSM tree turns random writes into sequential ones using a memtable, SSTables, and compaction
What write amplification and read amplification mean, with realistic numbers
Why both designs need a write-ahead log (WAL) to survive crashes
How to pick an engine from the workload: read-heavy vs write-heavy

steps.title: One write, two philosophies
steps.body: Your app saves one 100-byte row. Disks, both spinning and SSD, like big sequential writes (data laid down in order) and dislike many small scattered ones. A storage engine is the part of a database that puts data on disk. It must keep data sorted so reads are fast, yet still absorb writes cheaply. There are two main answers: the B-tree, which updates data in place, and the LSM tree, which never updates in place and merges later. Watch where each one pays.
steps.idea: A storage engine balances three costs: write cost, read cost, and space.
steps.caption: The app has one row to save and two possible engines.

steps.title: B-tree: edit the page in place
steps.body: A B-tree keeps sorted rows in fixed-size pages (8 KiB in Postgres, 16 KiB in InnoDB). To change one row, the engine finds its page, edits it, and later writes the whole page back, even for a 100-byte change. With 16 KiB pages that is up to about 160x write amplification (about 80x for 8 KiB). Write amplification means bytes physically written divided by bytes the app asked to write. Several edits to one page often share one flush, so real numbers are lower. Pages sit at scattered disk locations, so these are random writes. With the upper tree levels cached in RAM, a lookup costs about 1 disk read.
steps.idea: B-trees make reads cheap and predictable but pay for random, page-sized writes.
steps.caption: One small row change forces a whole 16 KiB page to be rewritten.

steps.title: Write-ahead log first
steps.body: Edited pages sit in RAM for a while, so a crash could lose them. To prevent that, in a durable setup both engine types first append a small record to a write-ahead log (WAL) and fsync it, which forces it onto disk. (Some engines let you relax this for speed.) The append is sequential, so it is fast. Only then does the engine acknowledge the write to the app. After a crash, the log is replayed to rebuild the lost changes. Extra mechanisms, such as full-page writes, also guard against half-written pages.
steps.idea: The WAL buys durability cheaply: one sequential append before anything else.
steps.caption: The log record is made durable before the app gets its ack.

steps.title: LSM: write to memory
steps.body: An LSM tree (log-structured merge tree) takes a different route. After the WAL append, the row goes into the memtable, a sorted structure in RAM (often a skip list). No data page is read or modified on disk. The write costs one sequential log append plus one in-memory insert, typically a millisecond or less on a local SSD depending on the fsync policy. So far each byte is written about once (write amplification 1x). Unlike a B-tree update, there is no page to find first and none to flush later. The sorting and merging work is postponed.
steps.idea: LSM writes touch only the log and RAM, so they are fast and sequential.
steps.caption: The row goes to the log, then into the sorted in-memory memtable.

steps.title: Flush to an SSTable
steps.body: When the memtable fills up (RocksDB defaults to 64 MiB), it is frozen and written to disk in one sequential pass as an SSTable. That is a sorted, immutable file (never edited again, so it is easy to cache and copy), usually with an index and a Bloom filter, a small structure that quickly says 'not in this file'. Each byte has now been written twice, to the log and to the SSTable (2x). The matching WAL segment can be deleted, because its data is safe on disk. New writes go to a fresh memtable.
steps.idea: Flushing turns many random updates into one big sorted sequential file.
steps.caption: The full memtable is written out as an immutable level-0 SSTable.

steps.title: Reads must look in many places
steps.body: A key may live in the memtable or in any SSTable, and newer data hides older data. So a lookup checks the memtable first, then the level-0 (L0) files, which are the freshly flushed ones and can overlap (4 here), then one file per deeper level. Read amplification means how many files or pages one lookup must check. Each SSTable's Bloom filter says 'definitely not here' quickly, so most files are skipped. Without filters a lookup could touch 8 or more files; with them it is about 1 to 2 disk reads.
steps.idea: LSM reads pay read amplification; Bloom filters keep it to about 1 to 2 disk reads.
steps.caption: The lookup checks newest data first and skips most files using Bloom filters.

steps.title: Compaction cleans up
steps.body: In the background, compaction merges overlapping SSTables into larger sorted ones at the next level. The 4 L0 files become 1. It drops overwritten values and deleted keys (tombstones, which are delete markers). This keeps reads fast and frees space, but every byte is rewritten several times as it moves down. With a size ratio of 10 (each level 10x bigger than the one above), leveled compaction typically lands around 10 to 30x write amplification, a rule of thumb that varies. Size-tiered compaction writes less but leaves more files and more duplicate data (space amplification).
steps.idea: Compaction is the bill for fast writes: the same data is rewritten again and again.
steps.caption: Compaction merges files and rewrites them one level lower.

steps.title: A write burst outruns compaction
steps.body: Imagine a bulk import writes faster than compaction can merge. Level-0 files pile up (24 here), and each lookup must check more of them, so reads slow down. To protect itself, the engine eventually slows or stops accepting writes (a write stall) until compaction catches up. Tuning compaction speed and file limits is a core LSM operations job. Bloom filters hide most of the cost for point lookups, but range scans and cache misses get noticeably slower.
steps.idea: LSM trades smooth latency for throughput; a lagging compaction shows up as slow reads and write stalls.
steps.caption: Compaction falls behind: L0 files pile up and writers get stalled.

steps.title: Pick by workload
steps.body: B-trees update pages in place: strong, predictable reads and range scans, but pricier random writes. LSM trees buffer writes in memory and merge sorted files later: very high write throughput and compact storage, but read amplification and compaction work. Both use a WAL for crash safety. Write-heavy ingest favors LSM; read-heavy transactional work usually favors B-trees. The write-amplification figures (80-160x for tiny B-tree updates, 10-30x for leveled LSM) are rules of thumb. Postgres and InnoDB use B-trees; RocksDB, Cassandra and HBase use LSM trees.
steps.idea: No free lunch: you choose where to pay, at write time (B-tree) or in the background (LSM).
steps.caption: Two engines, same goal, different places to pay.

quiz.q: A B-tree engine uses 16 KiB pages. An update changes a 100-byte row and the page is written back alone. Roughly how large is the page-level write amplification?
options: About 1x, only the changed bytes are written
quiz.why: 16,384 bytes written for 100 bytes changed is about 160x. In practice several changes to the same page may share one flush, so real numbers are lower.

quiz.q: What does an LSM write avoid that a B-tree update eventually has to do?
options: It writes only to the log and RAM, with no data-page read or rewrite on the write path
It skips the write-ahead log and relies on RAM alone
It writes each row straight to its final sorted position on disk
It waits for compaction to finish before it accepts the write
quiz.why: Both engines log to the WAL first. The B-tree must also find, modify and eventually flush a whole page at a random location, which may need a random read first. The LSM defers ordering work to flush and compaction.

quiz.q: An LSM database was fast, then after a huge bulk load its point lookups slow down and L0 file count keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
options: The memtable is too small to hold any rows
Compaction is falling behind the write rate
quiz.why: Many overlapping L0 files mean each lookup checks more files. That points to compaction not keeping up, and writers may soon be stalled.

quiz.q: The LSM engine holds recent writes in RAM. Why does it still write every change to a WAL?
options: RAM contents vanish on a crash, so the log lets the engine replay unflushed writes
quiz.why: The memtable is volatile. The WAL is a durable, sequential record of writes not yet flushed to an SSTable, replayed after a crash.

quiz.q: A service writes 50k small events per second and rarely reads them back by key. Which engine fits best?
quiz.why: Write-heavy ingest with few reads suits an LSM tree: writes are cheap and sequential, and the read amplification rarely matters.

cheatsheet.def: Sorted tree of fixed-size pages updated in place. Predictable reads and range scans; random, page-sized writes.
Writes go to a memtable, then flush to immutable sorted files merged in the background. Great write throughput.
Write-ahead log: sequential, fsynced record of each change before it is applied, replayed after a crash.
Memtable is the sorted in-RAM buffer; an SSTable is an immutable sorted file on disk, typically with an index and Bloom filter.
Bytes physically written divided by bytes the user wrote. Leveled LSM often runs 10 to 30x; B-trees pay it per page.
Number of places (files or pages) checked per lookup. Low for B-trees; LSM reduces it with Bloom filters and compaction.
Background merge of SSTables that drops overwritten and deleted data (tombstones). Keeps reads fast and limits space amplification (stale data lingering on disk), costs CPU, I/O, and rewrites.
Small probabilistic structure that says a key is definitely not in a file, so lookups skip it. Can give false positives, never false negatives.
